list.listitem: Dry eye syndrome (DES) usually can be diagnosed by clinical history. C
DES may be a symptom of an autoimmune disorder. C
Medications, environmental humidity, and eye use can be addressed to lessen symptoms. C
Artificial tears and ointments used ad libitum can treat symptoms. B

background.definition: DES (also called keratoconjunctivitis sicca) is a disorder of the tear film that causes damage to the ocular surface and is associated with symptoms of ocular discomfort and fluctuating vision.

list.listitem: 7.8% of women and 4.7% of men over 50 years of age are affected in the United States.
Inclusion of less severe cases would markedly increase these numbers.
Changes occur in vision, work capacity, and quality of life.
Causes of DES are varied; they may be multiple and may be idiopathic.
Systemic autoimmune disease (Sjogrens syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma, thyroiditis, graft vs. host disease).
Meibomian gland dysfunction.
Decreased tear secretion and blinking due to diminished corneal sensation (from trauma, surgery, neurologic disorders, herpes zoster, prolonged contact lens use).
Prolonged computer use, reading, or television watching.
Large palpebral fissure width, which can be hereditary, due to post-lid surgery, or associated with thyroid disease.
Hormonal changes, hormone replacement therapy, oral contraceptive use, and pregnancy.
Age-related changes decreasing blinking frequency and androgen levels.
LASIK surgery or eyelid surgery.
Topical and systemic medications (anticholinergic agents, beta blockers, antihistamines, corticosteroids, diuretics, isotretinoin, chemotherapeutic agents, antidepressants).
Trauma with scarring such as chemical burns or after Stevens-Johnson syndrome leads to loss of mucin production and epithelial damage even with preserved tear production.
Chronic viral infections (hepatitis C, human immunodeficiency virus).
Surgery (bone marrow transplants, head and neck surgery).
Radiation of orbit.
Infiltrative disorders (amyloidosis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, hemachromatosis).
Neurologic conditions that impair blinking.
Environmental conditions (decreased ambient humidity, temperature extremes, excessive wind, exposure to ocular irritant fumes).
Nutritional deficiency, particularly vitamin A.

Decrease in secretion of tears and an increase in tear osmolarity, resulting in instability of the tear film with break up between blinks, loss of its protective properties, leading to damage to the ocular surfaces, and symptoms of irritation.
Decrease in the sebum produced by meibomian glands. This oily layer normally retards tear evaporation.
Sandy, gritty, irritative dry eye symptoms that are worse as the day progresses suggest a lack of lacrimal gland tears. C
Symptoms that are worse after sleep or have a second peak much later in the day suggest meibomian gland dysfunction with loss of the superficial oil layer derived from sebum secretion. C
Irritative symptoms despite frequent use of artificial tears should raise suspicion that the topical medication is the cause of the symptoms. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Associated arthritic, systemic, constitutional features of the disease
Decreased blinking, mask-like facies, gait and motion disturbances
History of medication changes, radiation exposure, eye surgery
Exophthalmos, other symptoms and signs of thyroid dysfunction
History of fifth nerve trauma, surgery, long-term contact lens use; also aging, topical medications

list.listitem: Patients typically present with a sandy, dry feeling, or irritation; patients may have a history of exacerbating conditions such as excessive computer use or reading, dry environment, or medications that worsen symptoms (anticholinergic drugs, antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants).
Response to topical eye therapy, including improvement of symptoms with artificial tears or lubricants, or worsening of symptoms when products with preservatives are used, supports the diagnosis.
Obtain history of contact lens wear, schedule, and care; allergic conjunctivitis; and previous eye surgery history, including LASIK.
Obtain history of Bell's palsy, inflammatory disorders, dermatologic disorders, and dry mouth.
Older patients may be more likely to experience symptoms due to decreased blinking, arthritis, smoking, or estrogen use.
Schirmer test measures tear flow. Sensitivity and specificity are unknown, but false positive and false negative results are common.
Fluorescein staining can reveal areas of decreased tear volume.

Rose Bengal staining can reveal defects in the mucous layer. The changes over time can help in following disease progression of both aqueous and lipid secretion defects, and by measuring evaporative (tear breakup) time, indexes can be helpful in diagnosis and monitoring of disease progression and treatment response.
Order anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor, and other tests for autoimmune diseases if these are indicated by symptoms and examination.
Order thyroid function tests if symptoms of thyroid dysfunction are indicated.
Patient history is the main diagnostic tool to determine the cause of DES and appropriate therapeutic options.
Previous use of ocular lubricants with sustained relief may support the diagnosis.
Apply artificial tears ad libitum and at least 4 times a day. B
Humidify environment, limit or adjust computer use, avoid prolonged reading and contact lens use, and address other contributing factors. C
Eliminate causative medications. C

Artificial tears used ad libitum are the mainstay of treatment when decreased tear production is the primary defect. Based on mostly low quality evidence from 43 RCTs involving 3497 patients, a Cochrane review concluded that over-the-counter (OTC) artificial tears may be an effective and safe treatment for DES, but no specific formulation appears superior. More rigorous trials are needed and may change these conclusions.
Ointments used at night are useful adjuncts when meibomian gland dysfunction or incomplete lid closure occurs.

Tetracycline (doxycycline, minocycline) by mouth helps treat posterior blepharitis and meibomitis with or without ocular rosacea. After 3 months of treatment, the dose can be tapered to the lowest effective dose. Some patients may require some treatment indefinitely for acceptable control of symptoms.

Cyclosporine drops (0.05% or 0.1% twice daily) may be an option for patients with moderate to severe DES. However, a Cochrane review of 30 RCTs found little to no difference between topical cyclosporine (CsA) and vehicle or artificial tears for improving patient-oriented outcomes (ie, ocular discomfort) and disease-oriented outcomes (ie, ocular surface and tear film parameters) in the short-term. Moreover, CsA may increase adverse events like burning. Long-term studies are recommended for CsA.

Topical corticosteroids, based on a Cochrane review of studies with moderate to very low certainty evidence, may lead to small to moderate symptom improvement compared to CsA and lubricants. There is insufficient evidence for its efficacy for disease-oriented outcomes like tear film quality or quantity. And more importantly, its long-term adverse effects (eg, IOP elevation, cataract formation/progression) are very uncertain. Until high-certainty evidence is available, topical corticosteroids should not be used routinely for patients with DES.
Autologous serum eye drops have uncertain benefits for DES, based on a Cochrane review of 5 RCTs enrolling 92 patients.
Punctal occlusion by insertion of plugs into the lacrimal ducts is a treatment in severe cases. However, a Cochrane review of 18 RCTs involving 711 participants, showed uncertain benefits.
Tarsorrhaphy (surgical lid closure) is a treatment of last resort for persistent epithelial defects or corneal ulcerations.
Humidify the air at home and at work.
Hot compresses with a warm clean washcloth for 30 seconds 2 to 4 times a day improve meibomian gland function.
Limit contact lens wear.
Lower the computer screen to allow more of the eye to be covered with the upper lid.
Address lid hygiene with a dilute nonirritating shampoo, as indicated for seborrhoeic blepharitis, to reduce flaking and irritation.
If preservatives in eye medications are suspected, all treatments should be discontinued to determine whether symptoms resolve.
A trial randomized 299 adults with mostly moderate to severe dry eye to lubricant eye drops or "laughter therapy" (instructions here). Laughter therapy was non-inferior to lubricant eye drops.
Acupuncture has been studied with inconclusive results due to small sample size.
Omega-3 and omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation for treating DES have uncertain benefits, based on a Cochrane review of 34 RCTs involving 4314 patients.

LipiFlow Thermal Pulsation System, an externally-applied eyecup device, appears to have similar efficacy to comparators (ie, warm compress, eyelid massage, 5% lifitegrast, doxycycline), based on a Cochrane review of 13 RCTs (deemed low to very low certainty evidence).
Patients not responsive to first-line treatments or with any signs of visual loss should be referred to specialty treatment.
Patients with symptoms due to scarring trauma, postsurgical, or postradiation should also be referred to specialty treatment.
Control of symptoms and monitoring of disease progression are usually attainable goals in mild and moderate cases. C
Decreasing or eliminating medications and environmental triggers can greatly ameliorate symptoms. C
Severe disease warrants ophthalmology referral. C
Control of symptoms and slowing or elimination of disease progression are the goals.

Patients need to be educated about the chronicity and fluctuating course of the disease. They should also be taught about warning signs such as visual deterioration or escalating needs for more frequent use of artificial tears that might herald irritation caused by topical medication.
